sentences: Against a dark background, a girl glances back over the shoulder, lips slightly parted, as if we have just caught her attention.
Her eyes meet ours directly, as though someone had called her name a moment ago.
Johannes Vermeer of Delft painted this around 1665, yet it is not a portrait of a specific person.
It is a tronie, a Dutch genre for studying exotic costumes and expressions, painted on a canvas less than 45 centimetres tall.
The background, black today, was once a deep green curtain.
A 2018 research project revealed traces of a translucent green glaze laid over painted folds.
Its plant-based colours have faded over the centuries and darkened.
Look at the turban wrapped around her head.
Its blue is ultramarine, a pigment ground from lapis lazuli and known to have been more costly than gold at the time.
It shifts from sky blue in the light to deep indigo in shadow.
Now come closer to her eyes.
A tiny dot of light sits in each moist pupil and keeps her gaze alive.
The same research even found fine eyelashes, far too delicate to see with the naked eye.
Her parted lips also catch tiny dots of light.
These small highlights, as if she were about to speak, breathe life into the whole painting.
The moist red at the corner of her mouth is the warmest note in her face.
Lean in and look closely at the famous pearl: it has no outline at all, only a soft reflection of her white collar below and a single bright highlight above.
There is not even a hook attaching it to her ear.
A length of yellow cloth falls from the top of the turban down behind her shoulder.
Vermeer's estate inventory listed two tronies painted in the Turkish fashion, and this painting may well be one of them.
Below, the white collar and ochre jacket are handled very simply, with broad, loose strokes.
Set against the delicacy of the face and the pearl, this plainness quietly sends your eye back up toward her face.
In 1881 this painting, then in poor condition, sold at auction in The Hague for just over two guilders.
Its buyer had no heirs and bequeathed it to the Mauritshuis in 1902, where it still hangs today.
Vermeer lets your eye complete the rest, and that is the magic of the painter of light.
Step back, and see whether the pearl still looks perfectly round and solid to you, even though it is only a few touches of paint.
